how-a-deploy-ships-an-older-commit.html.text:
← Deploy Concurrency Check

How a deploy ships an older commit

Most pipeline bugs announce themselves with a red check. This one does the opposite: both runs go green, and the wrong one is live. Here is what each of the five patterns looks like from the outside, and why the evidence is so hard to find afterwards.

The shape of it

You push commit A. A minute later you push B. Both trigger the deploy workflow, and both runs start, because nothing told them not to.

  • 10:00 — A’s run starts. It waits four minutes for a runner.
  • 10:01 — B’s run starts. A runner is free immediately.
  • 10:04 — B finishes. B is live. Green check on B.
  • 10:09 — A finishes. A is now live. Green check on A.

Nothing failed. Both runs did exactly what they were asked to do, and neither one is aware the other existed. The branch shows two green checks in commit order, so the obvious reading — the newest commit is deployed — is wrong, and nothing on the page says so.

What makes it expensive is the debugging. The symptom arrives as “the fix I shipped isn’t live”, and every place you would look to check that — the commit, the check, the run log — says it is. The usual next step is to push again, which often fixes it, because this time the runs did not overlap. That turns a reproducible bug into an intermittent one, and an intermittent deployment bug can survive for years.

1. No concurrency group at all

The default. GitHub Actions runs whatever is triggered, in parallel, and does not serialize deployments for you — not even two runs of the same workflow, and not even two jobs naming the same environment:. Environment protection rules gate whether a deployment proceeds; they are not a queue. 

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false

That is the whole fix for this one. Runs that share a group name never overlap: the second waits for the first, so they apply in the order they were queued.

2. A group that is different on every run

This is the one worth knowing about, because it is invisible in review. The block is present, it is spelled correctly, and it does nothing: 

concurrency:
  group: deploy-${{ github.sha }}   # a new group every single run

A concurrency group only serializes runs that land in the same group. Key it on the commit, the run id, the run number or the attempt and every run gets a private group, so no run ever waits for another. The behaviour is identical to having no block at all — but now there is a block to point at, and the next person to read the file concludes the question has been dealt with.

It usually arrives by copying a CI workflow, where group: ci-${{ github.ref }} is correct and useful, and then changing the key while keeping the shape. github.ref and github.workflow are stable across the runs you want serialized; github.sha is not.

3. cancel-in-progress on a deploy

For a test run this is the right setting and saves real money: a superseded run has nothing to protect, so cancelling it costs only the minutes it had already spent. A deploy is not like that. By the time the cancel signal arrives it may have uploaded 300 of 900 files, applied a migration the new code has not shipped for yet, or replaced half a symlinked release directory. The run stops where it is, and nothing comes back to finish it.

The result is a state neither commit produced, which is worse than either of them being live. For a deploy, queue instead: 

  cancel-in-progress: false

4. Two groups for one target

A repository with a push-triggered deploy and a manual workflow_dispatch deploy usually has two workflow files. Each one is internally correct — each declares a concurrency group, each queues rather than cancels — and the two group names are different, because nobody wrote them at the same time.

A group is only a queue for the runs inside it. Two names means two queues means no ordering between them, so a manual deploy and an automatic one can write to the same target simultaneously. Reviewing either file on its own shows nothing wrong, which is exactly why this survives: the defect is in the relationship between the files, and no file contains it.

The same thing happens inside one file when two jobs name the same environment: and each carries its own job-level concurrency:.

5. Deploying a branch name instead of a commit

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    ref: main          # resolved when the step runs

A branch name is a pointer, and it is read at the moment the step executes — not when the run was queued. A job that waited twenty minutes for a runner checks out whatever main means twenty minutes later. A re-run of last week’s deploy, clicked to “redeploy that version”, deploys today’s.

This one is less about ordering than about identity: the run says it deployed commit A because A triggered it, and it shipped the tree at C. The run log records the ref, not the commit it resolved to, so afterwards there is often nothing that says which code went out. 

  with:
    ref: ${{ github.sha }}

Questions

Why does a deployment race not show up as a failed check?

Because nothing fails. Both runs do exactly what they were asked to do, and neither is aware the other existed. The branch ends up showing two green checks in commit order, so the obvious reading — that the newest commit is what is deployed — is wrong, and nothing on the page says so. The run that applied the older code does not report overwriting anything, because from inside that run nothing was overwritten.

Why is a per-run concurrency group worse than no concurrency block at all?

The behaviour is identical: no run ever waits for another. The difference is that now there is a block to point at. A reviewer who sees a correctly spelled concurrency section with an obviously well-intentioned group key ticks the line off, so the defect is protected by the thing that looks like its fix. It usually arrives by copying a CI workflow, where keying the group on the ref is correct and useful, and then changing the key while keeping the shape.

Why should a deploy queue instead of cancelling?

By the time a cancel signal arrives, a deploy may have uploaded 300 of 900 files, applied a migration the new code has not shipped for yet, or replaced half a release directory. The run stops where it is and nothing comes back to finish it, so the result is a state neither commit produced — which is worse than either of them being live. Queueing makes the newer run wait and then apply last, which is the order you wanted.

Why can two correct workflow files still race each other?

A concurrency group is only a queue for the runs inside it. A repository with a push-triggered deploy and a manual deploy usually has two files, each declaring a group, each queueing rather than cancelling, and the two group names differ because nobody wrote them at the same time. Two names means two queues, which means no ordering between them. Reviewing either file alone shows nothing wrong, because the defect is in the relationship between the files and no single file contains it.

Why is deploying a branch name a problem if the branch is correct?

A branch name is a pointer read at the moment the step executes, not when the run was queued. A job that waited twenty minutes for a runner checks out whatever that branch means twenty minutes later, and a re-run of last week's deploy clicked to redeploy that version deploys today's. The run log records the ref rather than the commit it resolved to, so afterwards there is often nothing that says which code actually went out.

Does adding concurrency make a deployment safe?

No. Serializing runs makes them apply in queue order, which is what you want almost always. It does not make a deployment atomic, it does not help if the deploy step itself is not idempotent, and it does nothing about a target that pipelines outside this repository also write to. It is the cheapest correct thing, not the last word.

Why concurrency is not the whole answer

Serializing runs makes them apply in queue order, which is what you want almost always. It does not make deployment atomic, it does not help if the deploy step itself is not idempotent, and it does nothing about a target that several pipelines outside this repository also write to. It is the cheapest correct thing, not the last word.

index.html.text:
Find the race that ships an older commit

A deploy that races itself does not fail. It succeeds — twice, in the wrong order — and what is left behind is a green check on the newer commit sitting above a live site running the older one. Paste a GitHub Actions workflow below and this page names every way yours is permitted to do that, with the line and the fix. Free, no sign-in, and nothing you paste leaves your device.

Paste one workflow at a time. Nothing is uploaded — the scan runs in this page.

Findings

Nothing scanned yet. Paste a workflow above, or load the example to see what a report looks like.

The five things it looks for

  1. No concurrency group on a deploying job. Two pushes run at once and the one that finishes last is the one that is live.
  2. A group that changes every run — keyed on github.sha, github.run_id and friends. Every run gets its own group, so nothing waits for anything. The dangerous one, because the block is there and reads as protection.
  3. cancel-in-progress on a deploy. Right for tests, wrong for a deploy: a cancelled deploy has already written part of its change and nothing re-runs to finish it.
  4. Split groups on one environment. Two jobs, or two workflows, writing to the same target under different group names do not serialize against each other at all.
  5. A deploying job that checks out a moving branch. A branch name resolves when the step runs, so a queued or re-run job can ship a different tree than the one it was queued for.

Read the longer version, with what each failure looks like from the outside, in how a deploy ships an older commit. There is also a comparison against reading the workflows yourself.

Run it in your own CI

The same logic ships as check.py — Python standard library only, no dependencies, no network access, and no GitHub token. A test in this repository runs both over the same workflows and asserts they report the same findings, so the CLI and this page cannot drift apart. 

python3 check.py .github/workflows/          # scan them all
python3 check.py .github/workflows/ --fail-on-risk   # exit 1 on a high-risk finding
python3 check.py deploy.yml --json          # stable ids, for your own tooling

Questions

What is a deployment race?

Two runs of the same deploy workflow overlapping in time. Push commit A, then commit B a minute later, and both runs start. If A's run happens to finish last — because it queued for a runner, because its build was slower, because a step retried — then A is what is live, while B's green check sits at the top of the branch. Nothing failed, and the run log for A does not say it overwrote anything, because from inside that run nothing did.

Does a concurrency block always fix it?

Only if the group name is the same for every run that writes to the same target. A group keyed on something that changes each run puts every run in a group of its own, so nothing ever waits for anything. That is the same race as having no block at all, with the difference that the block is there and reads as protection, which is why it survives review. Two workflows deploying the same environment under two different group names have the same problem for the same reason.

Should a deploy use cancel-in-progress?

Usually not. Cancelling is right for tests, where the only cost of stopping a superseded run is the time it had used. A deploy cancelled part-way through has already written part of its change — some of a batch of uploaded files, half a copied artifact, a migration that ran without the code expecting it — and nothing re-runs to finish it. For a deploy, queueing the newer run instead means it applies last, which is the order you want.

Is anything I paste uploaded?

No. The scan runs in this page's own JavaScript, on your device. Nothing you paste is sent anywhere, stored on a server, or logged. This page makes no network request of any kind after it loads — no analytics service, no font, no CDN. The same logic ships as a stdlib-only Python script with no network access at all, if you would rather not paste a workflow into a web page.

Can I run this in my own CI?

Yes. The CLI takes workflow files or a directory of them, prints the same findings this page shows, and can exit non-zero when a high-risk finding is present, so it can gate a pull request. It is free, MIT-licensed, has no dependencies beyond the Python standard library, and never calls the GitHub API.

Limits, and what this is not

This is evidence, not a determination. It reads the YAML you give it and reports patterns that permit an out-of-order deployment. It cannot know whether your deployment target is idempotent, whether a deployment protection rule already serializes the environment, or whether your team has decided a given race is acceptable. A clean report means this tool found none of the five patterns above — not that your pipeline is safe.

It is not a security audit, a compliance control, or professional advice, and no liability is accepted for any loss arising from its use or from a deployment you make after reading it. Verify anything it reports against your own workflows before changing them.

Privacy: everything you paste stays in your browser. This page uploads nothing, sets no cookie, embeds no third-party script, font or analytics service, and makes no network request at all once it has loaded. It keeps a small local count of how often the scan button is used, on your device only, which never leaves it and which you can switch off here:

vs-reading-your-workflows-yourself.html.text:
← Deploy Concurrency Check

This tool vs. reading your workflows yourself

You can find all of this by opening the files. The honest question is not whether you could — it is whether anyone will, on the day a workflow changes, across every file that writes to the same target, while already knowing which five patterns to look for. That is the gap this page is about.

Where reading it yourself is better

For one file, once, by someone who knows the failure modes, reading is strictly better and this tool adds nothing. You are not limited to five patterns. You know whether your deploy step is idempotent, whether the target has its own locking, and whether your team has already decided a particular race is acceptable — three things a scanner cannot know and will not ask. It will also miss anything outside its five checks and say nothing about it, which is the failure mode of every checker.

So this is not a replacement for reading your pipeline. It is a floor underneath it.

Where it stops working

One of the five is not in any file

Two workflows deploying the same environment under different concurrency group names is a defect in the relationship between two files. Each file is internally consistent and reviews clean. You only see it by holding both at once and comparing one string in each — which is a thing a person does badly and a scan does perfectly.

A reading is true for one day

The review happened. Then someone added a second deploy job, or copied the workflow for staging, or changed the group key while fixing something else. None of those diffs looks like “reintroduce a deployment race”, and none of them triggers another read of the whole set. Wiring the check into the pull request is what makes the answer current rather than historical: 

python3 check.py .github/workflows/ --fail-on-risk

The worst pattern looks correct

group: deploy-${{ github.sha }} is the expensive one, and it is expensive precisely because reading finds it only if you already know. The block is there, the syntax is right, and the intent is obvious and good. A reader who has not previously lost an afternoon to it ticks the line off. A check does not need to have lost the afternoon.

Which to use when

SituationWhat to do
One deploy workflow, and you are already reading itRead it. Use the five patterns as a checklist; you do not need this tool.
A dozen workflow files, several of which deploy somethingScan the directory — the cross-file finding is the one reading reliably misses.
You want the answer to stay truecheck.py --fail-on-risk in the pull request that changes a workflow.
Someone reports “my fix isn’t live” and the check is greenScan first. It takes seconds and rules this class out or in before you start reading logs.
You need to know if the deploy step itself is safe to interruptNeither. That is a property of your deploy script, and no workflow scan can see it.
You want a compliance artifact or an auditNeither. This is evidence for an engineer, not a control or an attestation.

Questions

Why not just read the workflow myself?

For a single file you should, and you will find most of this. The two places reading breaks down are scale and recurrence. Scale: a repository with a dozen workflow files has to be read as a set, because one of these defects — two workflows deploying the same environment under different concurrency group names — is not present in either file. Recurrence: the reading is only true for the day it was done, and a workflow that gains a second deploy job six months later reintroduces the defect against a review that already happened.

What does a checker see that a careful reader does not?

Nothing, on one file, read carefully, by someone who already knows all five patterns. That last clause is where the value is: the pattern that costs the most — a concurrency group keyed on something that changes every run — looks correct to a reader who has not been caught by it before, because the block is present and correctly spelled. A checker does not have to have been caught by it before, and it reads the twelfth file as carefully as the first.

Can I run the check automatically instead of visiting a page?

Yes, and that is the point of the CLI. check.py takes a directory of workflows and --fail-on-risk exits 1 on a high-risk finding, so it can run in the same pull request that changes a workflow. That converts the reading from something someone has to remember to do into something that happens on the diff that would have introduced the problem. It is Python standard library only, with no network access and no GitHub token.

Does the checker replace understanding the problem?

No, and it is not built to. Every finding names the line, explains what goes wrong in terms of what a user would see, and prints the fix, because a finding you do not understand is one you will either apply wrongly or suppress. The explainer page is there for the same reason. A team that reads the findings and then decides a given race is acceptable for their target has used this correctly.

What it costs you either way

Nothing, in both directions. This page is free, has no sign-in, no account and no usage limit, and it uploads nothing — the scan runs in your browser and this page makes no network request once loaded. The CLI is MIT licensed, depends on the Python standard library alone, and never calls the GitHub API or reads a token. If you would rather not paste a workflow into any web page at all, use the CLI; the two are held to identical output by a test that runs both over the same files.

Check a workflow, or read how a deploy ships an older commit.
